In the end, everyone wins.

1. We're tracking the last two bears closely. Both July 2018 and July 2022 were counter-trend rally months that gave it all back in the months that followed. We're in one now. The burden of proof sits with "this time is different," and so far the cyclical behaviour is just repeating.

2. The drawdown is shallow. ~50% off the high. 2018 ran 84%, 2022 ran 77%. History says there's a bit more at least.

3. No forced selling event. Dec 2018 and Nov 2022 each had a liquidation cascade with a name attached, a week where a large amount of BTC changed hands under duress. We haven't had one. Does it need to be another FTX? No. But something usually forces that transfer before a macro bottom prints.

4. We haven't touched realized price. Realized price is  the average price at which all BTC in supply last moved onchain and it sits around $52,5k. MVRV is 1.19.

Every prior bear traded below it. 2018, 2022, and the two before that all bottomed with MVRV under 1, meaning the average holder was underwater. We've not tagged it this cycle.

5. Macro looks questionable. AI trade has cooled, indexes are rolling and we have a sticky inflation theme. Won't take much for near term positioning unwind. Uncertainty at best. 

The biggest reason to be optimistic here is the ETF era moved a large block of supply into a cost basis that doesn't behave like 2018 or 2022 retail. If that's right, tagging $52k without piercing, or getting close to it is exactly what a mature BTC bear looks like.

As I have said many times, you can take all the emotion out of it at this point in the bear and simply run DCA.exe over the coming months. The 200W MA is clearly a solid long term entry point. 

Picking a macro bottom is a fun intellectual exercise and unnecessary for performance over cycles.

AI is moving beyond proposing scientific experiments and into the systems that run them.

Self-driving labs make that possible by connecting AI models to laboratory equipment. The result of each experiment feeds back into the model and shapes what it tests next.

Between the model and the machines sit two software layers with distinct roles. Execution orchestration converts the model’s plan into instructions the instruments can follow. When the run ends, data orchestration records how the experiment was performed and returns the result to the model.

This part of the stack is getting crowded. Frontier AI companies are building scientific agents and laboratory connectors, while hardware manufacturers are packaging their instruments into more integrated systems. The five largest are estimated to control 45–60% of lab-automation hardware revenue.

That leaves less room for companies whose only job is coordinating the equipment.

The data layer looks different. With every completed run, the system accumulates a deeper experimental history that gives the model more context for its next decision. A competitor may be able to replicate the scheduling software. Building the same depth of experimental history takes much longer.

The stronger advantage may be owning the data that informs the next experiment.

As someone who's obviously a very vocal bull on Collector, Beezie and onchain collectible platforms, a lot of people have reached out these past days asking for my thoughts on $FWA.

TLDR: exciting, but bearish.

Let me explain:

FWA is fascinating to me, but probably not for the reason most people are aping it.

It's another data point proving just how strong the pmf for gamified commerce really is. The excitement around the gacha mechanic is undeniable, and that part I'm extremely bullish on.

But people need to start differentiating. Because there's a massive difference between gamifying assets people genuinely want, and engineering a ponzi to manufacture demand for something nobody actually wanted in the first place.

$FWA gamifies NFTs, a market hardly anyone has shown any interest in anymore. It then uses heavy token emissions to subsidize participation and manufacture the appearance of demand. "Loss to earn" says it all, really.

Compare that to gamifying Pokémon cards, watches, or whiskey. Things people collected and loved long before crypto existed, and will keep collecting long after. That demand is real, and it doesn't need a token to exist.

And that's the whole tell. If you need a token to incentivize usage, the organic demand was never there. Non-crypto people don't get lured in by token emissions. They show up for products they actually want, and that's it.

FWA might print strong revenues right now, but I wouldn't be surprised to see those numbers back at 0 in just a few weeks. The big difference between FWA and platforms like Collector and Beezie is simple: one is a short-lived, trendy online casino trying to extract from gamblers, while the others are gamified commerce platforms serving genuine collectors with a superior UX.

Bullish on gamified commerce and everyone building products meant to last on top of it. Bearish on ponzis dressed up as innovation, as much as I love a good onchain experiment.

Tell someone outside crypto that their life savings depend on 24 words they can never lose, mistype, photograph, leak, or forget and they'd assume the product was broken.

In crypto, we somehow turned that into the standard.

You're expected to be your own bank and your own security team and your own archivist, forever. One slip years from now can still wipe the whole thing.

I went through Bron’s Seed Phrase Museum and took the security quiz myself.

It labelled my setup Cautious Collector, which is basically a polite way of saying I’ve done some things right, but there are a few gaps.

That was more useful than I expected because seed phrase risk usually feels abstract until a quiz starts asking where you store it, who knows about it, and what happens if that setup fails.

The Museum also tracks more than $7.2B in documented losses, but what got me wasn’t the size of the number.

It was how normal most of the mistakes are: a screenshot syncing to the cloud, bad handwriting, a damaged backup, or someone forgetting the password protecting it.

That made Bron’s mobile app easier to understand. It doesn't generate a seed phrase at all.

Its 2-of-3 MPC setup splits key control between your device, Bron and an independent third party, so one lost or compromised piece isn't enough to take the wallet down.

A system holding serious money shouldn’t require museum-level preservation skills from the owner.
It should survive normal people making normal mistakes sometimes.

Curious what everyone else gets with their quiz: https://t.co/Na3J5WBpon

Glad to partner with @bronwallet on this one.

You're expected to be your own bank and your own security team and your own archivist, forever. One slip years from now can still wipe the whole thing.

I went through Bron’s Seed Phrase Museum and took the security quiz myself.

It labelled my setup Cautious Collector, which is basically a polite way of saying I’ve done some things right, but there are a few gaps.

That was more useful than I expected because seed phrase risk usually feels abstract until a quiz starts asking where you store it, who knows about it, and what happens if that setup fails.

The Museum also tracks more than $7.2B in documented losses, but what got me wasn’t the size of the number.

It was how normal most of the mistakes are: a screenshot syncing to the cloud, bad handwriting, a damaged backup, or someone forgetting the password protecting it.

That made Bron’s mobile app easier to understand. It doesn't generate a seed phrase at all.

Its 2-of-3 MPC setup splits key control between your device, Bron and an independent third party, so one lost or compromised piece isn't enough to take the wallet down.

A system holding serious money shouldn’t require museum-level preservation skills from the owner.
It should survive normal people making normal mistakes sometimes.

My increasingly strong opinion is that compute is the biggest moat in AI.

Scientific breakthroughs don’t stay secret for long. Papers get published, researchers move, ideas leak, open source catches up. Give it enough time and almost everyone has access to roughly the same algorithms.

What doesn’t diffuse nearly as fast is the ability to run 10x bigger training runs, collect 10x more RL experience, serve billions of inference tokens, and iterate faster because you can afford thousands of experiments in parallel.

Scaling compute is brutally hard. It’s GPUs, power, substations, networking, cooling, land, permits, supply chains… and hundreds of billions of dollars. You can’t just decide to build that overnight.

The more I look at the industry, the more it feels like the frontier is less about having one genius idea and more about who can compound compute the fastest. Scaling laws reward whoever can keep scaling. That’s a very hard moat to replicate imo!
